projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Hal Biers was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: This interview is being conducted at the Fort Wayne VA Medical Center. The interviewer is Angie Roman of Senator Lugar's staff, and the interviewee is Mr. Hal Biers who served with the Army Air Corps during World War II, and was then called back again in Korea. His highest rank was a Master Sergeant. And his date of birth of January 21, 1922. Okay. Mr. Biers, we're ready to begin.

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: Start with how you got in the service. Were you drafted, or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: No, I volunteered.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: And why did you volunteer?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: Well, my high school class and everybody else was volunteering, and they belonged to the Guards, and I didn't. I was -- I decided I would join 'cause I figured there was gonna be a war very shortly and -- so I joined.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: And you chose Army Air Corps?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: Well, I went into the -- at that time you went into the regular Army and then you took a test. At Fort Thomas, Kentucky, I took a test and passed it. They put me in the Air Force. I didn't like the idea of sloshing around the infantry.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: Why did you choose to enlist in the Army as opposed to the Navy?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: Um, I really don't know. I just did. I enlisted in the Army because that's where all my buddies from high school, such as that had gone into. They had gone in the Army.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: Do you remember your first few days during basic training and your instructors?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: No, that's been about 50 some odd years ago. I really - I -- I had a little bit -- shall we say, a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: Tell me what you remember about your service.

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: Oh, I remember many things about the service. I went all over the United States at first for about the first part of 19 and 41, and -- I mean the latter part of '41, first part of '42. I took my basic in Wichita Falls -- at Sheppard Field in Texas. Then I went to Jackson, Mississippi. From Jackson, Mississippi, I went to Columbia, South Carolina. And then I -- at base photograph -- they came through and wanted a combat photographer so I applied for it. About two weeks later I -- they accepted me and sent me to Roy Rogers Field, Oklahoma City. And then from there they sent me to Lowry Field and gave me a brush up on photography, because I had worked as a young man in photography. Then I went to Pittsburgh, California, overseas about two weeks later to Townsville, Australia. From there I started up through New Guinea. And I laid in Nadzab, New Guinea, and then I started in -- I -- first I covered -- Finschhafen was the first New Guinea assault that I was in, and then went to Finschhafen - I went to Hollandia rather. From there to Wewak and Wewak to Noemfoor and then went to Bougainville. From Bougainville I went to Lae. From Lae I went to Luzon. After Luzon I went to Borneo. Then I ended up in Ie Shima , same place I took the picture of Ernie Pyle right after he was killed. I had a picture of him. And the story you wanted me to tell -- I'd like to tell you why I'm such a flag lover. I went on up to this lava hill there in Ie Shima and we came up on a young Marine, 19 year old Marine from Michigan. He'd been mortally wounded and he -- some Marines had -- ahead of time had wedged the flag among some lava rocks up ahead. He had said to his squad leader -- he said would you move me over into the shadow of Old Glory so I can die a free man. I'll never forget that as long as I live. So for that reason -- I'm sorry. Every time I tell this I get a bit of feeling. That's an awful short time for 43 months in combat. That was my tour of duty in the South Pacific. Then I came back to San Francisco. I went back to Manila. We spent there about a month and-a-half, before they sent us back to the states there at Repo Depot, and we got to San Francisco and the dock workers were on strike, and we had to go south go down to port -- Los Angeles. Then before we -- we docked and then came back to Fort Wayne, Indiana, and I mean back not Fort Wayne but to Indianapolis and was discharged, and went home to Kentucky to where my family was. That was my tour of duty throughout World War II. That took a period of 43 months.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: Tell me about being a combat photographer. What happened to your photos?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: What we were actually -- we were -- the reason we was ground force instead of Air Force, General Arnold, Hap Arnold wanted a record of all -- anything that was affected by aerial activity. Well, hardly a squad ever went out in the Marines or the Navy or regardless of what it was that they didn't have aerial recon maps or photos of the area that they were going in to take. And then why -- that's the reason we were with the ground -- I was with the Marines -- with the more Marines more than anything else. I was with the Army. I was once with the Australians. And every picture that we took -- a copy of all the pictures went to OWI and the other one went to the Air Force -- or not the Air Force but Air Corps. I got to change it because I -- when I came back in the service in the Korean War it was the United States Air Force then. And the -- so we hit the beachhead. We had a stream of team. There was a lieutenant and two of us enlisted men. And we hit with assault troops and took pictures of everything you can think of. And as I said we processed -- a portion of the time we processed our own film in the -- in the -- ourselves and sent -- this was the pictures.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: And you did you that out in the field environment?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: Out in the field. I sent the negatives -- mostly sent negatives to the base -- base photo and from there it was forwarded on to the air -- to the -- to General Arnold, Air Force.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: Do you have copies of the photos you took?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: I had a lot of copies, but over the period of many years and all my kids and grandkids and such as that they looted my -- I do have a picture of Ernie Pyle as he was -- right after he was killed.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: Do you recall the day that your service ended?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: Really, no. Because I -- main thing I remember is that when I got back to Somerset, Kentucky, where my family was - why I remember that when I got off the train and Doggin Hines, one of my old buddies was there to meet me. I went up, saw my dad and brother at the shop that they owned. Then I saw my mother and such as that. I remember that very clearly, but as far as the last day in the service I guess that was -- in World War II, that would be as I said when I was discharged.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: When you were discharged did you go back to school or did you go to work or what did you do?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: I went back to photo portrait school. I became a portrait photographer. I went to Portageville, Missouri and run a picture studio for a short time. Then Olan Mills and Fox Studios, these chain outfits was coming through town and you couldn't keep up with them. So I went -- left, went in public relations, spent the rest of my life in public relations. I was executive secretary of the Chamber of Commerce.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: Tell us what you do now.

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: I'm retired and I volunteer at the Legion, Forty and Eight, and of all places the VA hospital.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: What did you do here at the VA?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: I work with the admitting, such as that. I got 16 years out here and over 6,000 hours as well. And I cook for -- bring in cakes for all the gals and guys that you might as well say this, have their birthdays. And then I -- once a month we have carry in down in admitting, and I bring the meat. Years ago I used to be a chef, and I got out of it because you work all the time. You don't have any time for your own self.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: Do you have anything else you want to add about your service that I haven't asked you about?

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: No, I enjoyed it. I mean a great portion of it I enjoyed, Not -- I wouldn't say -- I saw things that I don't even like to talk about the same as any other vet, and I -- only thing we talk about is the funny things that happened to us during our tenure in the service. I met a girl here in Fort Wayne and married her and took her back to California. I came -- they sent me - sent me here, as I said, to set up a base photographic lab out at Bear Field which is our air field here. And then as I said, they give me a chance to either getting out of the service or getting -- or getting married, so I chose the better of the two, I thought at the time anyway. I have three kids. I had four but I lost one of them. I can say this, that I feel as though that -- I'm glad to see something like this going on for the simple reason -- not for me -- but for the veterans. They - seems to be that when they get through with them they're through with them. And I have seen -- we held a memorial here in Fort Wayne for the 187 servicemen that was killed in the Pentagon, because everything that you saw on TV and everything else was the Twin Towers in New York. So we held a -- downtown in front of the square, Dr. Hayhurst and I put on a memorial for the 187 men. We -- it was fairly well attended. We felt a lot better that they would be getting some recognition -- I mean their families.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: I don't have any other questions. Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Angela Roman
sp.p: I appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Hal Biers
sp.p: Thank you.
